title: Chapter 212 – Forty to One
html:
[Hall of Ten Thousand Names – Mei]

The Ring has a pulse, and Mei has been counting it for twelve days.

She does it without meaning to, the way a person who lives beside a river stops hearing the water until the day it changes. Nine hosts, nine slow beats, nine small lights set in a circle behind her eyes. When the Print was cut, three weeks ago, the lights became a ring of warmth she could feel from the other side of the Hall, and she learned the rhythm of each one as she once learned the footsteps of her father in the corridor: Yue's, quick and bright; Hai Ren's, patient; Han's, restless; Cheng Hui's, dry and exact. And Jian's, which is the slowest of all, a deep steady knock like a hand on a door in another house.

For eleven days, it has been slowing down.

She noticed it on the second morning. She told herself she was tired. She noticed it again on the fourth, and told no one. By the seventh she had begun to lie awake in the dark, with her hand pressed flat to the stone floor of the alcove, counting.

Eight beats of Yue's heart to one of Jian's, at the start. Then sixteen. Then forty.

Today it is a little over forty. She counts it three times, to be sure, and then she gets up, and puts on her short robe, and goes to find Kuang.

---

The Hall of Ten Thousand Names is not quiet anymore.

That is the first thing that strikes her, every morning, as she comes down the long stair into the central gallery. When she first came here, in the spring, it was a vault, a place of cold air and dust and the faint paper smell of a great many sleepers. Now the air is warm. It smells of porridge and lamp oil and wet wool. The central floor is crowded with cots, and between the cots, in the thin gray light from the high windows, women and men and children move with the careful steps of the newly woken. Some are weeping. Some are asleep again. A boy of perhaps six sits on the end of a cot with a bowl in his lap and stares at the spoon as though it were a miracle.

Four hundred woke the first day. Nine hundred by the end of the first week. Two thousand and eleven names were on Kuang's roll at the start of the month, and Mei has stopped checking the number, because it goes up every time she looks away.

She finds Kuang at the long table by the east wall, surrounded by scrolls.

He does not look up. He is a lean old man with a stained sleeve and a pen tucked behind each ear, and he has been working eighteen hours a day since the Roll first woke. His eyes are red. His left hand, the one he writes with, is shaking.

"Two thousand, three hundred and fourteen," he says, to the scroll. "Counting the new babies. Not counting Perrin Ado's lot, who I'm told are still arguing about whether they're dead."

"Master Kuang."

"Mei." He lifts the pen from behind his right ear and uses it to point at the stool across the table. "Sit. Eat something. You look like a boiled sheet."

"I need to tell you something."

"Eat first."

"Kuang."

He looks up. She watches him take in her face, and for the space of a breath the clerk's mask comes off and he is simply a very old man who has seen too many people say that sentence in that tone.

"Ah," he says.

He puts down the pen.

---

She tells him in the alcove, because it is private, and because the bed is there, and because Little Mei is asleep in it.

The child lies on her side with one fist under her chin, a slight, dark-haired girl in a nightshirt too big for her, and her breathing is slow and regular. She looks, Mei thinks, exactly like a child who has been cured. She has been cured. Jian paid ten years of his life for it, and she has been sleeping, since, with the deep plain sleep of someone who has been very ill and is not any longer.

"The Ring is out of sync," Mei says.

Kuang sits on the end of the bed. He has brought the scroll; she supposes he cannot bring himself to leave it. "Explain."

"We are nine people with a shared pulse. When the Print runs, it draws on all nine at once, and the draw is steady because we beat in time. That's what the Interface needed. Nine hosts in rhythm." She keeps her voice level. "But Jian has gone up the Road, and the Road runs slow for him, or fast for us, and the Ring can't tell which. It's holding on. It's trying to keep the nine of us in step. And it's costing me."

"You are the Ring's anchor."

"I am the Ring's weakest member." She says it flatly. "My capacity was always the lowest. Five percent spare, on the last audit. It's lower now. I can feel it going, a little more each morning. It isn't pain. It's like holding your breath."

Kuang's face is gray.

"And the child," he says.

Mei looks down at Little Mei's sleeping face.

She has not told him about the two percent. She has not told anyone but Jian, and Jian is a long way off. It was a private thing, a thing between sisters, though Mei had not yet known she was a sister: a child of seven, lying in a nursery, pushing a little of her own strength across the dark to a woman she had known for a week. You were so tired, she said, afterward. I wanted to help.

"The child is lending me strength," Mei says. "She has been, since the first night. I didn't ask. She did it in her sleep. And I didn't stop her, because I thought—" She swallows. "I thought it was a small thing."

"Is it?"

"No." Her voice cracks. "It's the Lin blood fault. It was never cured, Master Kuang. It was only moved. When Jian printed the remedy fragment, he cured the sickness. But the fault is in the blood, and the blood is hers, and every time she gives me a little of what she has, the fault opens a little more."

Kuang is quiet for a long time.

"How long?" he says.

"At the present rate? Twenty days."

"That is not long."

"It's forty days to Jian's one," Mei says. "Twenty of ours is half a day of his." She bites her lip. "I don't think he knows."

---

Yue is waiting on the stair when they come out.

She has been there some time. Mei can see it in the stiffness of her stance, the way she has folded her arms across her ribs. Yue Zhao has been a hard woman to read for as long as Mei has known her, a lean, dark-eyed fighter with a tongue like a whetstone, and in the last weeks she has become harder, the way a blade is hard after a good many hours at the grindstone.

"I heard," she says.

"You were listening."

"I was standing on a stair. If you didn't want me to hear, you should have shut the door." Yue's mouth tightens. "Kuang. Give us a moment."

The old man looks from one to the other. He sighs, and picks up his scroll, and goes down the stair toward the cots.

Yue waits until he is out of earshot.

"You have to tell me what the Ring does," she says. "Not the version you gave the Council. The real one."

Mei hesitates.

"I'm the one he swore to tell first," Yue says, very quietly. "He didn't. Not about the Print, not about the remedy, not about whatever it is that he's carrying that he thinks I can't see. And he's gone, and I'm standing here with a hole in my chest the shape of a man who lied to me, and I would like very much to know how much of the dark I'm in."

"Yue—"

"Mei." Yue's voice breaks. She steadies it. "Please."

So Mei tells her.

She tells her about the nine hosts and the Interface's leak. She tells her what the Print draws on, and why, and what it means that the Ring has been losing a day, from each of them, every time the Print runs. She tells her about the slow pulse of Jian's heart across the Ring, and the forty-to-one, and what happens to a circle of nine when one of them is a very long way away and the others keep aging.

She does not tell her about the Lin blood fault. She tells herself it is not hers to tell.

When she is finished, Yue stands for a long moment with her hands clenched at her sides.

"Eight of us," she says.

"Yes."

"Eight of us holding up one, who is holding up the rest."

"Yes."

"And if we stop?"

"The Ring lets go. Jian loses the Print. He loses the Scan. He loses—" Mei stops. "Everything the Interface gives him, except what's already mended. He'll be a Core cultivator at eighty-two percent in the middle of the Road of Nine."

Yue lets out a long breath. When she speaks again, her voice is steady and very cold.

"Then we don't stop."

---

The Wall's messenger arrives at noon.

He is a boy of fifteen in a mud-spattered cloak, and he has ridden three days without sleeping. He is led into the central gallery, between the cots, with a guard on either side, and he stands in front of the long table with his chest heaving and presents a rolled and sealed strip of paper to the first person who holds out a hand.

It is Mei.

She breaks the seal. It is Wenyuan's script, small, upright, shaky, the strokes of a man writing with a tremor. She reads it once, and goes cold, and reads it again.

To the Hall of Ten Thousand Names. To Mei, and through her to the Nine.

The Wall holds. The Seam has been quiet for six days, which is longer than at any time since the tower was built. I do not trust it. I do not know why it is quiet. I think it has found something better to listen to.

Qinghe is well. She asks that you tell Kuang she still owes him a debt of broth. Elder Ye Shuhan has not returned. The Azure Cloud Sect's embassy waits at the gate. They have been told nothing. They are patient men, and I think they are afraid.

I will say what I have not said to anyone. I can feel Jian. Not through the Ring, which was never meant for me. Through the tower. He is climbing. He is moving through the Road at a speed I cannot measure. I think he is moving slowly. I think the world is moving very fast.

There are things on the Wall that I would have been glad to see. I do not think I will have time.

I am not in pain. I wish you to know that. The tower is very kind to me.

Wenyuan.

Mei reads it a third time, and then she folds it, and puts it in her sleeve, and finds that she is holding the edge of the table very hard.

"Is he well?" says the boy, hoarsely.

"He says so."

"He doesn't look well." The boy's eyes are enormous. "Not since the Elder died. He doesn't leave the tower now. The monks say his feet don't work. And his eyes—" He swallows. "They shine at night."

Yue has gone very still.

"Thank you," Mei says. "Go and eat. You'll be given a bed."

The boy goes. The guards follow. The gallery goes back to its murmur of spoons and soft voices.

Yue says, without turning her head: "I do not think I will have time."

"Don't."

"What time does he mean, Mei?"

She does not answer.

---

---

Perrin Ado is in the east annex, where the archivists have taken over a long room of scroll cabinets and turned it into a refuge for people who do not know whether they are alive.

He is a small, pale, fussy man of perhaps sixty, in a robe that has not been washed in two centuries, and he sits cross-legged on the floor surrounded by wax tablets and blank paper. He is writing. He has been writing since the morning he woke, a day-by-day account of everything he has seen, with the stubborn neatness of a man who believes that if a thing is recorded it cannot be taken away.

"Mei of the Nine," he says, without looking up. "I wondered when you would come."

She sits on the floor across from him. It is a small, cold, dusty room, and the tablets are laid out around him in rows, and she sees that he has drawn the Hall's floor plan in the margin of the nearest one, with every door marked.

"You said no," Mei says. "When the Roll was called. Kuang's notes say you were one of the ones who refused."

"I refused." Perrin sets down his stylus. His hands are very clean. "I was a coward. I'd spent three hundred years in a vault, and I'd made peace with it, and when the covenant was read I said, no, thank you, I'd rather stay asleep. It was a perfectly reasonable thing to say."

"And then?"

"And then something woke me anyway."

She waits.

"A voice," he says. "In the dark. It said my name. My real name, the one my wife used, which no one living has heard in a very long time." His mouth twists. "She's been dead six hundred years. And she said, Perrin, it's time to get up. There's porridge. The way she did, on the days I'd worked through the night."

Mei's skin crawls.

"I woke up with my face wet," Perrin says. "I was standing by my cot. The Roll was open, and Ishan Vael was calling me Captain, which I'm not, and there was porridge." He laughs softly. "I thought: well, that's that. I'm alive again. How lovely. How very kind of someone."

"It was the Tenth," Mei says. "That's what Kuang said."

"That's what I said. I said it to Hai Ren, when she asked, and she wrote it down." He picks the stylus up again, and turns it over in his fingers, and does not write. "But I've had twelve days to think, and I have a confession. I don't believe it was him."

"Why not?"

"Because the voice asked for nothing."

Mei goes still.

"Everyone I've ever loved asked me for something," says Perrin Ado gently. "My wife asked me to eat. My mother asked me to write. My Master asked me to be honest, and it nearly ruined me. Love is a thing that costs. I have tried for twelve days to think of a single time anyone I loved did a kindness without a price." He lifts his eyes. They are a faded, gentle brown. "And I can't. Not one. So I'm afraid I think something wore my wife's voice to wake me up. And I'm afraid it did it for a reason."

"What reason?"

"I don't know." He sets down the stylus. "But there is a thing I did hear, Mei of the Nine, when I was between sleeping and waking. It said my name. And then it said something else, in a different voice, very softly. Something I wasn't supposed to hear."

"What?"

"It said, Is that enough?" says Perrin Ado. "And another voice answered, from a long way off. And it said: No. Keep going."

Mei stays with him for another hour. She writes down what he tells her, in the margins of her own notes, and she gives him her thanks, and she goes out into the long gray corridor with her hand pressed to her mouth.

---

Tian Mo finds her there.

He is leaning against the wall opposite the annex door with his arms folded, in the plain gray tunic of the Hall's new guard, and he has the look of a man who has been waiting a while and has decided not to mind. He is a broad, weathered young man with a scar through one eyebrow, and the soldiers who woke on the first day have taken to calling him Captain, whether he likes it or not.

"The Sect embassy," he says. "They've reached the lower gate."

"Already?"

"They've been on the road eleven days. They traveled fast." His mouth is flat. "Forty riders, in the pale blue. Their leader says he is Elder Ye Shuhan's second."

"Ye Shuhan is on the Road of Nine."

"I know. I told him." Tian Mo shifts his weight. "He didn't believe me. He wants to speak to whoever is in charge. He wants to see the Roll. He wants—" He hesitates. "He wants to know what became of six pupils of the Sect, who were sent to the Wall at the end of last season and have not been heard from."

Mei closes her eyes.

Lan Xiu, she thinks. Five stone. One alive.

"Tell him," she says, "that the matter is in hand."

"Is it?"

"No."

"I thought not." Tian Mo's voice is level. "I can hold the gate. I have forty men and a good wall and the memory of what the Sect did the last time they were refused. But I'd like to know what I'm holding it for."

She opens her eyes.

"Sit," she says.

He sits on the floor beside her, with his back to the wall and his knees drawn up, and they look together at the long gray corridor and the arch of the high window and the dust turning slowly in the light.

"I need you to do something," says Mei. "And I need you not to ask me why."

"That's a very large favor."

"I know."

"Go on."

"There's a child in the east alcove," Mei says. "She isn't well. And in a little while there may be a good deal of noise. I'd like you to keep the Sect out of the building for three days. Whatever they say. Whatever they offer."

Tian Mo thinks about it.

"Three days," he says.

"Three."

"And what do I tell them?"

"That the Hall is under quarantine for a sickness we cannot name." She meets his eyes. "It will be perfectly true."

---

She writes to him that evening, knowing he will not read it.

It is a habit she picked up in the first days at the Hall, when she was new and afraid and Jian was only a name on a ledger. She would sit in the alcove by the lamp with a scrap of paper and a stub of charcoal and write down what she could not say, and then burn it in the stove, and feel lighter. He never knew. She does not think he would have minded.

Jian, she writes. I think I have made a mistake, and I do not know how to take it back.

She stops. The charcoal is a small black weight in her fingers.

I should have told you about the child. I should have told you about the Ring. I should have said it was costing me more than I let you see, because you have a way of carrying everything on your own, and I thought if I kept my share small, you would have less to carry.

It does not work like that. I know that now.

Perrin Ado says love is a thing that costs. I think he is right. I think the voice that calls you up the stair is the one that asks for nothing, and the ones that love you are the ones that ask, and are afraid to, and ask anyway.

So I am asking.

She writes the last line very slowly, and looks at it for a long time.

Come home. Whatever it costs. Come home.

She feeds the paper to the stove. The flame takes it, curls it, turns it white, and for a moment, in the low light, she thinks she sees the ash hold its shape. A line of small black letters on a leaf of ash, rising on the warm air toward the vaulted dark, as though somebody very far away were reaching down to read it.

Then it crumbles, and is gone.

---

That night, the Ring breaks.

It does not break dramatically. There is no sound, no flare of light. She is sitting on the end of Little Mei's bed with a bowl of cold porridge on her knee, trying to eat, when the pulse in the back of her head stumbles, and goes on, and stumbles again.

She puts down the spoon.

She closes her eyes and reaches for the circle, the way she has reached ten thousand times, and for a moment everything is as it was: the eight warm points, bright and steady. Yue's, in the corridor. Han's, far away, on the Wall road. Hai Ren's, in the lower hall. Tian Mo's, a rough pale spark. And the slowest of all, the deep dim knock of a hand on a faraway door.

Then the knock falters.

It misses one beat, and then another. It does not stop. It slows, like a pendulum in a stopped clock, and the space between each pulse stretches until it is minutes long, then hours, and the dim light behind her eyes pulls thin.

Jian, she thinks, and reaches harder.

She feels something give.

It is a small, soft, almost tender sound, like the snapping of a thread in a worn cloth. The Ring is a circle of nine, and one point of it has gone out of reach, and the other eight are now holding a gap. For a moment the gap is a pressure, an ache, a dark hollow where a man's heartbeat has been. Then it closes, and the Ring tightens around the hole like skin around a splinter, and she understands that it has done what it was built to do.

It has let him go.

She opens her eyes.

Little Mei is awake.

The child lies on her side, with her eyes wide and dark in the lamplight, looking up at her. She does not speak. She has the unnaturally still face of a child who has understood something too large.

"You felt it too," Mei says.

Little Mei nods.

"It's all right." Mei puts her hand on the thin, hot shoulder. "It isn't your fault. It was never going to last, a thread that long. It's only—it's only that he can't—"

"Is he dead?"

"No."

"Are you sure?"

"Yes." Mei hears her own voice, steady and false. "He's just very far away. He's somewhere the Ring can't reach."

The child studies her for a long moment. She has a way of looking, this small girl, that Mei has begun to recognize: a trick of the eyes, an old, tired patience. It is not a child's look. It is the look of someone who has been awake in the dark a great many years, and has learned to see who is lying.

"I gave you some more," Little Mei says.

"What?"

"Yesterday. When you were asleep. I gave you some more, so you wouldn't be so thin." Her voice is very small. "I'm sorry. I didn't ask."

Mei stares at her.

She does the arithmetic in her head. Twelve days. Two percent, on the night of the first lending. Another on the fifth, perhaps. Another yesterday. She has been so careful. She has been counting the Ring's pulse and not the child's.

"How much?" she whispers.

"I don't know." Little Mei's lip trembles. "It didn't hurt. It was only warm."

Mei reaches for the child's wrist and finds the pulse, and counts.

Thirty-one. Forty. A skip. Forty-eight. A skip. A beat so faint it is almost not there.

She counts again.

And somewhere below them, in the crowded gallery, a boy of six drops a spoon, and it rings on the stone floor, and the sound goes up through the high vaulted dark like a note from a cracked bell.

"Mei?" says Little Mei. "Mei, I'm cold."

Mei does not remember standing up. She does not remember lifting the child. She remembers only the weight of her, light as a handful of straw, and the sound of her own voice, rising, saying a name that was never meant to be shouted in the Hall of Ten Thousand Names:

"Yue! Yue!"

And the stair shaking as someone starts to run.
